title: World Religions & Wisdom
description: A respectful, balanced introduction to the world's religious and cultural traditions: festivals, special places, founders and teachers, sacred texts, rites of passage, shared values, and the academic study of religion and freedom of belief. Each tradition is described as its followers understand it, with beliefs, traditions and historical evidence clearly labelled. Learners are invited to understand, not asked to adopt any belief.

lessons.title: Lamps, Candles and Lights
objectives: Name three festivals that use lights
Say one way each festival is celebrated
prerequisites: Knows that families celebrate special days
explanation: Many people around the world celebrate festivals with lights in the darkest or coldest time of year.

At Diwali, Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and some Buddhists light small clay lamps called diyas. Many Hindus remember Rama coming home to Ayodhya. At Hanukkah, Jewish families light one more candle each night for eight nights on a special candle-holder called a menorah (hanukkiah).

At Christmas, Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus, and many homes are decorated with lights and stars. Different festivals, different stories — but lots of families enjoy light, food and being together.

context.text: Diwali, Hanukkah and Christmas each have their own stories and customs, celebrated in many different ways by different families.
For believers, these festivals remember sacred events: Rama's return for many Hindus, the rededication of the Temple for Jews, and the birth of Jesus for Christians.

vocabulary.meaning: a special day or time of celebration
to do something happy for a special day

examples: Lighting diyas and making rangoli at Diwali.
Spinning a dreidel at Hanukkah.

story.title: Three Windows
story.text: On one street, Ivaan saw three glowing windows. In the first, his family's diyas flickered in a row. In the second, his neighbour Sarah lit the fifth candle on her menorah. In the third, the Fernandes family switched on their star lantern. "Everybody's window is bright!" Ivaan said. Sarah waved and smiled.

lessons.title: Thank You for the Harvest
objectives: Explain what a harvest festival is
Name harvest festivals from different places
explanation: A harvest is when farmers gather the crops they have grown. Many people hold festivals to say thank you for the food.

In Tamil Nadu, Pongal is celebrated by cooking sweet rice in a new pot until it boils over — a sign of plenty. Across India, Makar Sankranti is celebrated with kites and sesame sweets. In Korea, families celebrate Chuseok with rice cakes called songpyeon.
In the United States and Canada, families gather for Thanksgiving dinner. Jewish families build a hut called a sukkah for Sukkot. All these festivals remember that food is a gift to be grateful for.

context.text: Harvest festivals are celebrated at different times of year depending on local crops and calendars.

examples: Flying kites and eating til-gul at Makar Sankranti.
Saying thank you before a meal.

story.title: The Pot Boils Over
story.text: Grandma placed the new clay pot on the fire. Rice, milk and jaggery bubbled inside. "Watch!" she said. The milk foamed higher and higher until — whoosh — it spilled over the top. "Pongalo pongal!" everyone cheered. "When it boils over, it means a year full of good things," Grandma explained.

lessons.title: Where People Pray
objectives: Match traditions to their places of worship
Describe how to show respect when visiting
prerequisites: Knows different families celebrate different festivals
explanation: Many traditions have special buildings where people gather to pray, sing, learn and meet. Hindus visit a mandir (temple), Sikhs a gurdwara, Muslims a mosque (masjid), Christians a church, Jews a synagogue and Buddhists a vihara or temple.
Each place has its own customs. In many mandirs, gurdwaras and mosques, people take off their shoes. In a gurdwara, everyone covers their head. In a mosque, people wash before prayer.
When we visit someone else's special place, we follow its customs, speak quietly and ask questions politely.

context.text: Customs vary between communities and buildings; it is always best to ask what is expected.

vocabulary.meaning: showing love and respect to God or what is holy

Removing shoes before entering a mandir.

story.title: The Visit
story.text: Ivaan's class visited a gurdwara. At the door, everyone took off their shoes and tied on orange head-scarves. Inside, beautiful music filled the hall. Ivaan sat quietly on the carpet. Afterwards, a kind uncle explained the holy book, the Guru Granth Sahib, and invited them to share a meal. "Thank you," Ivaan whispered politely.

lessons.title: Everyone Eats Together
objectives: Explain the Sikh langar
Describe sharing food in different traditions
explanation: In every gurdwara there is a free kitchen called the langar. Anyone can eat there, whatever their religion or background. Everyone sits together on the floor as equals. Volunteers cook, serve and wash up.
The langar was started by Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, more than 500 years ago. The Golden Temple in Amritsar serves free meals to many thousands of people every day.
Other traditions share food too: at Eid al-Adha, many Muslims share meat with family, friends and people in need. In Hindu temples, food offered in worship, called prasad, is shared with everyone.

context.text: The langar is a central Sikh institution expressing equality and selfless service (seva).
The Golden Temple's langar is widely reported to serve tens of thousands of people a day, and more on festival days.

vocabulary.meaning: a free community kitchen in a gurdwara

examples: Volunteers rolling rotis in the langar.
Sharing sweets with neighbours at a festival.

story.title: Ten Thousand Rotis
story.text: At the Golden Temple, Ivaan watched volunteers rolling rotis faster than he could count. A grandmother, a businessman, a student and a tourist all sat side by side on long mats. A boy his age poured him dal. "Who pays?" Ivaan asked. "Nobody," his mother smiled. "Here, everyone is a guest, and everyone can help."

lessons.title: Three Teachers from India
objectives: Describe the lives and key teachings of the Buddha, Mahavira and Guru Nanak
Distinguish historical evidence from tradition
explanation: Siddhartha Gautama, who became the Buddha ("the awakened one"), lived in northern India about 2,500 years ago. Tradition says he left his palace to understand suffering, meditated under a Bodhi tree and taught the Middle Way between extremes.

Mahavira, a teacher of the same era, is the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism. He taught ahimsa — non-violence towards all living beings — so strictly that some Jain monks sweep the path to avoid harming insects.

Guru Nanak (1469–1539), born in Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib, Pakistan), founded Sikhism. He taught that there is one God, that all people are equal, and that people should work honestly, share and remember God.

context.text: Historians accept the Buddha, Mahavira and Guru Nanak as historical figures; the Buddha's and Mahavira's exact dates are debated.
Many details of their lives, such as the Buddha's four sights, come from later traditional accounts.
Followers regard their teachings as paths to liberation or union with God.

vocabulary.meaning: in Buddhism, awakening to the truth
in Jainism, a great teacher who shows the way to liberation

examples: The Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya.
Guru Nanak's teaching "Kirat karo, naam japo, vand chhako" — work honestly, remember God, share.

story.title: The Four Sights
story.text: According to tradition, young Prince Siddhartha had never seen suffering. One day, riding outside the palace, he saw an old man, a sick man, a funeral and a calm wandering monk. Deeply moved, he left his comfortable life to search for an answer to suffering. Years later, under a tree at Bodh Gaya, he found the peace he had been seeking.

subtopics: Treat others as you wish to be treated

lessons.title: Treat Others as You Would Like to Be Treated
objectives: Find versions of the golden rule in several traditions
Apply the golden rule to real situations
explanation: Many traditions teach a version of the "golden rule": treat others the way you would want to be treated.

The Mahabharata says one should not do to others what would be hurtful to oneself. Confucius said, "Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself." Jesus taught, "Do to others as you would have them do to you." Rabbi Hillel said, "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour." A hadith says none truly believes until they wish for their brother what they wish for themselves.
The golden rule is a simple test: before acting, imagine being the other person.

context.text: Versions of the golden rule appear in the Mahabharata, the Analects of Confucius, the Gospels, the Talmud and the hadith, among others.
Philosophers note limits: people may want different things, so some prefer "treat others as they would wish to be treated".

vocabulary.meaning: treat others as you want to be treated
an idea about what is important
treating each other in the same way

examples: Sharing because you would like others to share with you.
Not teasing because you would not like to be teased.

story.title: The Swap Test
story.text: Kiko wanted to grab the best swing. Then he remembered his teacher's "swap test": imagine you are the other person. He pictured himself waiting while someone else hogged the swing. Kiko stepped back. "You go first, then me?" The other boy grinned. They took turns all break and became friends.

The golden rule says…

lessons.title: Books Held Holy
objectives: Match sacred texts to their traditions
Describe how different traditions treat their sacred texts
explanation: Most religions have sacred texts. Hinduism has many, including the Vedas, Upanishads and Bhagavad Gita. Judaism has the Torah and the wider Hebrew Bible (Tanakh). Christianity has the Bible, including the Old and New Testaments. Islam has the Quran, which Muslims believe was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad.

Buddhism has collections such as the Pali Canon (Tipitaka). Sikhism has the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs treat as their living Guru — it is placed on a raised platform, covered with cloth and fanned with a chauri.
Many texts were passed on orally before being written down. The Vedas, for example, were memorised with remarkable accuracy for centuries.

context.text: Followers often regard their texts as revealed, inspired or authoritative.
Scholars study when and how texts were composed; for example, the Rigveda is commonly dated to roughly 1500–1000 BCE.
Vedic chanting has been recognised by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

vocabulary.meaning: a message believed to come from God
speaking a text aloud from memory

examples: The Guru Granth Sahib carried on the head with great respect.
Muslims learning to recite the Quran in Arabic.

story.title: The Memory Keepers
story.text: For centuries, before printing, families of Vedic reciters trained their children to memorise thousands of verses using clever patterns — reciting words forwards, in pairs and in loops — so not a single sound would change. Even today, some students train for years, keeping alive one of the oldest continuous oral traditions on Earth.

activities.prompt: Match the text to the tradition

A sacred text is called…

thinking: Why might people memorise texts instead of writing them?

speaking: Explain how one tradition treats its sacred text, using respectful language.

lessons.title: Marking Life's Milestones
objectives: Compare rites of passage in different traditions
Explain why communities mark milestones
explanation: Rites of passage are ceremonies that mark important changes in a person's life: birth, growing up, marriage and death.

Many Hindu families hold a naamkaran (naming ceremony) and the upanayana (sacred thread ceremony) for some children. Jewish young people celebrate a bar or bat mitzvah at 13 (or 12 for girls in some communities). Many Christians are baptised. Sikhs may take amrit in an initiation ceremony.
Weddings and funerals differ widely, but all help people celebrate, grieve and feel supported by their community.

context.text: Practices differ greatly within each tradition, between regions and between families.
Anthropologist Arnold van Gennep (1909) described rites of passage as having three stages: separation, transition and incorporation.

vocabulary.meaning: a ceremony marking a life change
a ceremony of joining a group
a formal event with special actions

examples: A first haircut ceremony (mundan) in some Hindu families.
A quinceañera at 15 in many Latin American communities.

story.title: Leah's Big Day
story.text: Leah practised for months to read from the Torah scroll in Hebrew for her bat mitzvah. On the day, her hands trembled as she began, but her voice grew steadier with each line. When she finished, her family and friends cheered and threw soft sweets. "Now you're responsible for your own choices," her grandfather said proudly.

activities.prompt: Match the rite to the tradition

lessons.title: A Map of World Traditions
objectives: Summarise key beliefs of major traditions accurately
Interpret data on religious affiliation
explanation: Scholars often group traditions into families. Abrahamic traditions — Judaism, Christianity and Islam — trace their roots to Abraham and believe in one God. Dharmic traditions from India — Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism — share ideas such as karma and dharma, though they interpret them differently.

East Asian traditions include Confucianism, Daoism and Shinto, often practised alongside Buddhism. According to Pew Research Center estimates for 2020, Christians made up about 29% of the world population, Muslims about 26%, Hindus about 15%, Buddhists about 4%, and the religiously unaffiliated about 24%.
Data have limits: people may belong to several traditions, practise without "believing", or identify culturally. Categories invented by outsiders do not always match how people describe themselves.

context.text: Figures are estimates from the Pew Research Center's analysis of global religious composition (2010–2020).
Groupings such as "Abrahamic" and "Dharmic" are scholarly categories, useful but simplified.

vocabulary.meaning: in Indian traditions, the principle that actions have consequences

examples: A Japanese family visiting a Shinto shrine and a Buddhist temple.
People identifying as "spiritual but not religious".

story.title: The Census Question
story.text: A researcher in Japan asked people, "What is your religion?" Many said "none". Yet the same people visited shrines at New Year and held Buddhist funerals. "Religion" for them meant joining a group, not practising customs. The researcher realised that a single question could not capture how people really live their traditions.

lessons.title: Traditions of Land and Community
objectives: Describe features of indigenous traditions
Explain the link between indigenous traditions and the environment
explanation: Indigenous traditions belong to particular peoples and lands. They are often passed on orally through stories, songs, dances and rituals, and connect people with ancestors, animals and the land.

In India, many Adivasi communities, such as the Bhil, Gond and Santhal, have their own deities, festivals and art forms. Sacred groves — patches of forest protected by communities for generations, such as the devrai of Maharashtra and the kavu of Kerala — have preserved rare plants and animals.

Aboriginal Australian peoples speak of the Dreaming, which connects law, land, ancestors and creation. These traditions are diverse and should be described in their communities' own words where possible.

context.text: Indigenous traditions are diverse; no single description fits all.
Ecologists have documented higher biodiversity in many protected sacred groves in India.
Terms like "Dreaming" are English translations that only partly capture Aboriginal concepts.

vocabulary.meaning: a term used by many indigenous communities of India
a forest protected for religious reasons
a family member from long ago

examples: Warli and Gond art telling community stories.
A devrai in the Western Ghats protecting old trees.

story.title: The Grove No One Cuts
story.text: In a village in the Sahyadri hills, there was a dark green grove where no one cut even a twig. "It belongs to the goddess," the elders said. When scientists visited, they found trees hundreds of years old, rare frogs and medicinal plants that had vanished elsewhere. Belief and tradition had protected a treasure for science.

goals: Use academic approaches to study religion

units.title: Studying Religion

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: How Scholars Study Religion
objectives: Compare insider and outsider approaches
Apply the concept of lived religion
explanation: Religious studies aims to understand religions without promoting or attacking them. Scholars distinguish insider (emic) perspectives — how followers describe their own beliefs — from outsider (etic) perspectives that use analytical categories.

Ninian Smart proposed seven dimensions of religion: ritual, narrative and mythic, experiential and emotional, social and institutional, ethical and legal, doctrinal and philosophical, and material. Max Müller, a 19th-century pioneer of comparative religion, famously said, "He who knows one, knows none."
Recent scholars study "lived religion" — what ordinary people actually do and feel in daily life, which may differ from official teachings.

context.text: Scholars debate whether "religion" is a universal category or a concept shaped by Western history.
Smart's dimensions appear in works such as "The World's Religions" (1989) and "Dimensions of the Sacred" (1996).

vocabulary.meaning: religion as practised in daily life

examples: Studying how families actually celebrate a festival.
Comparing official doctrine with personal practice.

story.title: Two Descriptions of One Ritual
story.text: A student described a family's Lakshmi puja two ways. First, as the grandmother explained it: welcoming the goddess of prosperity into a clean, lamp-lit home. Then, as an anthropologist might: a ritual reinforcing family bonds and economic hopes at the start of the financial year. "Both are true in different ways," her teacher said.

activities.prompt: Match the term
Who proposed seven dimensions of religion?
Scholars debate whether "religion" is a universal category.
"He who knows one, knows none" was said by…

thinking: Can an outsider fully understand a religion?
Why might lived religion differ from official teachings?
speaking: Describe a ritual from both emic and etic perspectives.

project.title: Lived Religion Study
steps: Observe or interview (with permission) about a family practice
Record the insider's explanation
Analyse it using Smart's dimensions
Write a 1500-word reflective report
project.safety: Obtain informed consent before observing or interviewing. Respect that religious practices are personal, allow participants to decline, and anonymise notes unless they agree to be identified.

assessment.prompt: Ninian Smart's model includes a material dimension.

lessons.title: Freedom of Thought, Conscience and Religion
objectives: Explain legal protections for freedom of belief
Compare models of secularism
explanation: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including the freedom to change one's religion or belief and to practise it.

India's Constitution guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion (Article 25), subject to public order, morality and health. The word "secular" was added to the Preamble in 1976. Indian secularism is often described as "principled distance" — the state may engage with all religions equally — while French laïcité emphasises strict separation.

Pluralism goes beyond tolerance: actively engaging with difference. Historical examples include Ashoka's edicts urging respect for all sects and Akbar's Ibadat Khana debates. Debates continue over how to balance religious freedom with equality and other rights.

context.text: Article 18 UDHR (1948); Constitution of India Articles 25–28; the 42nd Amendment (1976) added "secular" to the Preamble.
Scholars such as Rajeev Bhargava describe Indian secularism as "principled distance"; its practice is widely debated.

vocabulary.meaning: keeping state and religion separate or neutral
a person's inner sense of right and wrong

examples: Ashoka's Rock Edict XII on respect for other sects.
Interfaith dialogue groups in many cities.

story.title: The House of Worship Debates
story.text: In the 1570s, Emperor Akbar built the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri, where scholars of different faiths — Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian — debated questions of belief. The discussions were sometimes heated, but they reflected a remarkable curiosity about other traditions.

activities.prompt: Article 18 of the UDHR protects…
options: freedom of thought, conscience and religion

activities.prompt: Match the concept

thinking: How should a society balance religious freedom and other rights?

speaking: Lead a respectful discussion on different models of secularism.
